Key Research Thinking Patterns: Multimodal Imaging Fusion for Clinical Biomarkers: Integrating nuclear medicine imaging with computational segmentation to derive quantitative physiological metrics from non-invasive data. (e.g., Using an ensemble of U-Nets and sliding window filters on 18F-FLT PET/CT scans to automatically segment vertebral bodies and extract Standard Uptake Values for tracking bone marrow recovery in HSCT patients.)

Analytic Signal Decomposition for Dynamic Systems: Applying time-frequency analysis techniques to extract intrinsic mode functions from noisy or short-duration experimental data. (e.g., Utilizing the Mirror Periodic Method (MPM) and Hilbert Vibration Decomposition (HVD) to compute analytic-signal backbones from accelerometer data of single-degree-of-freedom oscillators, overcoming Hilbert transform end-effects.)

Transform Optimization for Data Compression: Designing novel mathematical transforms that balance computational efficiency with reconstruction fidelity for lossy coding standards. (e.g., Developing a 2D separable 8x8 Hirschman transform that is inherently real and integer-valued, demonstrating superior PSNR and quantization performance compared to standard DCT and H.264 integer transforms on video sequences.)

Spectral Band Fusion for Enhanced Detection: Leveraging multi-spectral sensor data to improve object detection performance, particularly for small targets where single-band systems fail. (e.g., Evaluating YOLOv4 on a dual-band infrared (DBIR) dataset to demonstrate a 50% improvement in recall for small object detection compared to longwave infrared alone.)
Summary Description: Joseph Havlicek is a multidisciplinary researcher specializing in the intersection of biomedical imaging, signal processing, and computer vision. His work focuses on developing non-invasive diagnostic tools for hematology, specifically using 18F-FLT PET/CT and deep learning segmentation to monitor hematopoietic stem cell engraftment and malignancy relapse. Concurrently, he contributes to fundamental signal processing through the development of novel integer-valued transforms for video compression and analytic signal decomposition methods for structural dynamics. His recent research extends to dual-band infrared object detection, enhancing small target recognition for autonomous systems. By integrating compartmental modeling, U-Net ensembles, and Hilbert transform techniques, Havlicek bridges clinical translational goals with rigorous mathematical and computational methodologies.
